Alice1.summary: <Theory> has unreasonable consequences because refraining from an action counts as an act that harms someone.

Bob1.summary: Doing nothing cannot be considered an act, so <Theory> does not imply that refraining from giving money caused harm.

Alice2.summary: Excluding omissions from being acts leads to unreasonable consequences, as not rescuing a drowning child clearly harmed the child.

Bob2.summary: An omission resulting from a deliberate decision is an act, so not rescuing the child is an act that caused harm, preserving <Theory>.

Alice3.summary: Treating deliberate omissions as acts still leads to unreasonable consequences, as keeping an intended gift does not seem to harm the recipient.

c1.text: Under <Theory>, for an act to cause harm to someone means that, if the act had not occurred, that person would have been in a better state.

c2.text: Under <Theory>, for an act to benefit someone means that, if the act had not occurred, that person would have been in a worse state.

c3.text: Alice chose not to give 50,000 won to a friend; had she given it, the friend would have been in a better state.

c4.text: Alice1 assumes that doing nothing, such as choosing not to give 50,000 won, is considered an act.

c5.text: Alice's not giving 50,000 won to her friend harmed her friend.

c6.text: It is unreasonable that not giving 50,000 won harmed the friend.

c8.text: Doing nothing, like simply not giving 50,000 won, cannot be considered an act.

c9.text: Alice's not giving 50,000 won is not an act and did not harm the friend under <Theory>.

c10.text: <Theory> does not imply that not giving 50,000 won harmed the friend.

c11.text: A person had the ability to rescue a struggling child but chose not to, resulting in drowning; had they rescued the child, the child would have been in a better state.

c12.text: Under Bob1's view of an act, not saving the child is not an act and thus did not harm the child.

c13.text: Not saving the child caused harm to the child.

c14.text: Excluding omissions from being acts leads to unreasonable consequences.

c15.text: An omission that is the result of a deliberate decision should be considered an act.

c16.text: The choice not to save the child was the result of a deliberate decision, so it is an act that caused harm to the child.

c17.text: A bought a gift intended for B, but deliberately decided to keep it instead of giving it to B.

c18.text: Had A given the gift to B, B would have been in a better state.

c19.text: A's not giving the gift to B was the result of a deliberate decision, so it is an act.

c20.text: A's not giving the gift to B caused harm to B.

c21.text: A's not giving the gift to B did not cause harm to B.

c22.text: Treating deliberate omissions as acts leads to unreasonable consequences.

h1.text: I could have punched my friend and broken their nose but did not do so; had I punched them, they would have been in a worse state.

h2.text: Not punching my friend is an act.

h3.text: By not punching my friend, I performed an act that benefited my friend.

a.note: Under Alice1's assumption that omissions are acts (c4) and Theory's definition of benefit (c2), refraining from breaking a friend's nose is an act that benefited the friend.

b.note: Checks whether Alice2 and Bob2 differ on c13 (not rescuing harmed the child). Both hold c13, so the conjunction is true and its negation is false.

c.note: Asserting c20 makes Bob's position inconsistent only if Bob's position also holds c21 (contrary of c20). Bob's rules derive c20 and do not derive c21, so Bob remains consistent.
